lead: Additive manufacturing makes a part by adding material in layers from a 3D model. This unit covers the standard process families, the CAD-to-part chain, and the main machines: SLA, FDM, powder bed fusion, LENS, LOM and jetting. After it, a student can classify an AM process, trace its steps, estimate simple build quantities, and choose rapid tooling or rapid manufacturing for a job.
about: This unit explains how parts are made by adding material layer by layer instead of removing or forming it. Chapter 7.1 gives the development, standard classification and benefits of additive manufacturing. Chapter 7.2 follows the common process chain from CAD model to finished part. Chapters 7.3 to 7.8 take the main processes one by one: stereolithography, fused deposition modelling, powder bed fusion and selective laser sintering, LENS, laminated object manufacturing, and the jetting family. Chapter 7.9 connects these processes to rapid tooling and rapid manufacturing. The chapters move from general ideas to individual machines, then to industrial use, so a student can classify a process, sequence its steps and choose it for a prototype or a tool.

chapters.idea: AM builds a solid part by adding material layer upon layer from a 3D model, so it is classified by how the layers are formed.
chapters.depth: Development from 1980s layer-by-layer models to functional parts; the term rapid prototyping versus additive manufacturing. Seven standard families: vat photopolymerisation, material extrusion, powder bed fusion, material jetting, binder jetting, sheet lamination, directed energy deposition. Benefits and limits: no part-specific tooling, complex internal channels, low-volume production, mass customisation; slow build, size limit, surface finish, support removal, material cost, anisotropy. Some syllabi call the whole group 3D printing.

figure.aria: A tree shows seven additive manufacturing process families branching from AM processes, with common example processes under each family.

chapters.example: A bracket needs a small batch. CNC setup costs ₹15,000 and each part costs ₹2,000; AM setup costs ₹2,000 and each part costs ₹3,500. Find the break-even batch size and which route is cheaper for 5 parts. A: 15,000 + 2,000n = 2,000 + 3,500n gives n = 8.67; at 5 parts AM costs ₹19,500 against CNC ₹25,000, so AM is cheaper.
chapters.trap: Do not classify AM only by material; the standard families are by layer-forming mechanism. 3D printing is an umbrella term, not one process.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3 basics of plastics; general manufacturing overview.
chapters.leave: Working details of SLA, FDM, SLS, LENS, LOM and jetting to Chapters 7.3-7.8.

chapters.idea: Rapid prototyping turns a CAD model into a physical model through a fixed chain: STL, orientation, slicing, layer build and post-processing.
chapters.depth: Rapid prototyping as a physical model for form, fit and function checks; why it shortens design iteration. Generic AM chain: CAD solid → STL surface mesh → orientation and support → slicing → layer build → removal, support cleaning, post-cure or finishing. STL facets, units and common errors; effect of build orientation on time, support and surface; layer thickness trade-off. Some syllabi call the chain the AM process chain.

figure.title: AM process chain
figure.aria: A vertical flow shows CAD model becoming an STL mesh, then orientation and support, slicing, layer build, post-processing and a finished part.

chapters.example: A cylinder is 40 mm tall and sliced at 0.2 mm. Find the number of layers. A: 40 / 0.2 = 200 layers; at 0.1 mm it is 400 layers.
chapters.trap: STL is a surface triangle mesh, not a solid voxel model; layer count is height divided by layer thickness, not volume divided by layer volume.

chapters.idea: Stereolithography cures a liquid photopolymer layer by layer with a UV laser or projector.
chapters.depth: Vat photopolymerisation: UV laser or projector cures liquid photopolymer on a platform. Laser, galvanometer scan, recoating blade, platform lowering, supports, post-cure. Layer thickness, resolution, resin types and applications. Some syllabi call this stereolithography apparatus (SLA); do not confuse with SLS.

figure.title: SLA build
figure.aria: A vertical flow shows a laser and mirror curing resin at the surface, then the platform lowering and the part being post-cured.

chapters.example: A part is 30 mm tall with 0.1 mm layers. Each layer has hatch length 4,000 mm and scan speed 500 mm/s. Find scan time. A: layers = 30 / 0.1 = 300; time per layer = 4,000 / 500 = 8 s; scan time = 300 × 8 = 2,400 s = 40 min, plus recoating and post-cure.
chapters.trap: SLA uses a liquid photopolymer, not a thermoplastic filament; the laser cures only the scanned area and overhangs need supports.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 7.2 process chain; basic polymer curing.
chapters.leave: Photopolymer jetting to Chapter 7.8; powder sintering to Chapter 7.5.

chapters.idea: Fused deposition modelling extrudes a melted thermoplastic filament through a moving nozzle, building the part as a stack of raster layers.
chapters.depth: Material extrusion: thermoplastic filament is fed by drive rollers, melted in a heated nozzle and deposited as a raster. Bed lowers, part grows. Materials: PLA, ABS, PETG, nylon, PEEK; support, layer height, infill, raster angle; anisotropy. Some syllabi use the trademark FDM; the standard family is material extrusion.

figure.title: FDM build
figure.aria: A vertical flow shows filament being fed, melted in a nozzle, deposited, the bed lowering and the part growing.

chapters.example: A part has 100 layers of 0.2 mm. Each layer path is 250 mm and print speed is 50 mm/s. Find build time ignoring travel. A: 100 × 250 / 50 = 500 s = 8.33 min.
chapters.trap: FDM is not sintering or curing; part strength depends on raster orientation, and layer thickness is not the same as nozzle diameter.
chapters.leave: Powder bed and jetting processes to later chapters.

chapters.idea: Powder bed fusion spreads a thin powder layer, then a laser or electron beam fuses only the chosen cross-section.
chapters.depth: Powder bed fusion: recoater spreads powder; laser or electron beam scans a cross-section and fuses particles; platform drops; repeat. SLS for polymers (partial melting), SLM/DMLS for metals (full melting), EBM variant. Unfused powder supports overhangs. Powder handling, thermal stresses and post-processing. Some syllabi call this laser powder bed fusion.

figure.title: Powder bed fusion
figure.aria: A vertical flow shows powder supplied, spread by a recoater, scanned by a laser, fused, and the platform lowering for the next layer.

chapters.example: A part layer area is 5,000 mm², hatch spacing 0.1 mm, scan speed 800 mm/s, layer 0.05 mm and height 20 mm. Estimate scan time. A: scan length per layer = 5,000 / 0.1 = 50,000 mm; time per layer = 50,000 / 800 = 62.5 s; layers = 20 / 0.05 = 400; scan time = 25,000 s = 6.94 h, plus recoating.
chapters.trap: SLS does not need support for overhangs because the powder bed supports the part; SLS is not the same as SLM for metals.
chapters.leave: Blown-powder LENS to Chapter 7.6; binder jetting to Chapter 7.8.

chapters.idea: LENS uses a laser melt pool on a substrate and blown metal powder to build or repair a part without a powder bed.
chapters.depth: Directed energy deposition: laser creates a melt pool on a substrate; metal powder is blown through a nozzle into the pool; CNC motion builds a track, layer by layer. Used for repair, cladding and near-net shapes. Materials: steel, titanium, nickel alloys. Some syllabi call this LENS or laser cladding; the standard family is directed energy deposition.

figure.title: LENS build
figure.aria: A vertical flow shows a laser and powder nozzle meeting at a melt pool, depositing a track on a CNC table to build or repair a part.

chapters.example: A worn shaft of diameter 50 mm and length 100 mm needs 0.5 mm radial build-up. Deposition rate is 20 cm³/h. Find time. A: volume = π(25.5² − 25²) × 100 = 7,933 mm³ = 7.93 cm³; time = 7.93 / 20 = 0.397 h = 23.8 min.
chapters.trap: LENS is blown-powder DED, not a powder-bed process; it needs a substrate and is not chosen for fine internal channels.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 7.5 powder bed contrast; Unit 4 laser welding melt pool.
chapters.leave: Powder bed fusion details to Chapter 7.5; welding defects to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Laminated object manufacturing bonds and cuts thin sheets layer by layer, then removes the excess material.
chapters.depth: Sheet lamination: thin sheets of paper, polymer, metal or ceramic are fed, glued, pressed and cut to the cross-section; excess material is cross-hatched for removal; layers stack. Laser or blade cutting. Advantages: low cost, large parts; limits: z-accuracy, delamination, finishing. Some syllabi call this laminated object manufacturing (LOM).

figure.title: LOM build
figure.aria: A vertical flow shows a sheet being glued, pressed, cut, the platform lowering, excess material removed and the part finished.

chapters.example: A 50 × 50 × 30 mm block is built from 0.1 mm paper sheets. Find layers and sheet area; if sheet costs ₹40/m², find material cost. A: layers = 30 / 0.1 = 300; area = 300 × 50 × 50 = 750,000 mm² = 0.75 m²; cost = 0.75 × 40 = ₹30.
chapters.trap: LOM bonds and cuts sheets; it does not melt powder or cure resin. Z-accuracy depends on sheet thickness and adhesive, and excess material must be removed.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 7.2; Unit 3 sheet metal and plastics sheet handling.
chapters.leave: Powder and jetting processes to other chapters.

chapters.idea: Jetting processes use printheads: material jetting deposits and cures liquid droplets, while binder jetting deposits a binder into a powder bed.
chapters.depth: Material jetting: printhead jets droplets of photopolymer or wax and UV-cures them; multi-jet modelling (MJM, PolyJet) uses many jets for fine layers and multi-material or colour parts. Binder jetting: printhead jets a liquid binder onto a powder bed; green part is cured, sintered or infiltrated. Compare with SLS (no binder) and SLA (vat resin). Applications: visual models, casting patterns, colour prototypes.

figure.aria: A tree separates jetting AM into material jetting with photopolymer, wax and multi-jet modelling, and binder jetting with powder bed, liquid binder and sintering or infiltration.

chapters.example: A binder-jetted part is 25 mm tall with 0.1 mm layers. The layer is 100 mm wide, printhead width is 10 mm and print speed is 200 mm/s. Find print time ignoring powder spreading. A: layers = 25 / 0.1 = 250; passes per layer = 100 / 10 = 10; time per pass = 100 / 200 = 0.5 s; time per layer = 5 s; total = 1,250 s = 20.8 min.
chapters.trap: Binder jetting uses no laser; the binder forms a green part that needs curing or sintering. MJM is material jetting, not FDM.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 7.1 classification; Chapter 7.3 photopolymer; Chapter 7.5 powder bed.
chapters.leave: SLS mechanism to Chapter 7.5; FDM to Chapter 7.4.

chapters.idea: Rapid tooling uses AM to make moulds, dies, inserts or patterns, while rapid manufacturing uses AM to make end-use parts.
chapters.depth: Rapid tooling uses AM to make or help make moulds, dies, inserts and patterns; rapid manufacturing uses AM for end-use parts. Direct tooling: AM insert with conformal cooling. Indirect tooling: AM pattern for investment casting, soft mould or bridge tooling. Economics, batch size, material and surface requirements; applications in injection moulding, casting and jigs. Some syllabi call this rapid tooling techniques.

figure.aria: A tree divides rapid tooling into direct tooling with conformal cooling and AM inserts, and indirect tooling with casting patterns, soft moulds and bridge tooling.

chapters.example: A conformal-cooled insert cuts injection cycle time from 30 s to 20 s for 10,000 parts. Machine hour rate is ₹500. Find time and cost saving. A: saving = 10 s/part × 10,000 = 100,000 s = 27.8 h; cost saving = 27.8 × 500 = ₹13,900.
chapters.trap: Rapid tooling is not the same as rapid prototyping; tooling can be indirect, and not every AM tool matches hardened steel life.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 7.1-7.8; Unit 1 casting patterns; Unit 3 injection moulding.
chapters.leave: Mould design and casting gating to Units 1 and 3.
